detailed_guide:
# Havelock & Port Blair Premium — Islands & Beaches (6D/5N) — Complete Travel Guide

## Overview

This is a six-day, five-night premium islands-and-beaches trip across Havelock (officially Swaraj Dweep) and Port Blair, the two anchors of the Andaman & Nicobar Islands. At ₹70,000 for two, it suits honeymooners, friends who want reef time without backpacker logistics, and first-time island travellers who would rather be driven than negotiate at a jetty. You stay at Radhanagar Bayview Resort, a 4-star resort and boutique property rated 4.6, with daily breakfast and one signature dinner included. Private sedan transfers and sightseeing cover the road legs, and a certified local guide joins the main sightseeing blocks. Entry and experience passes for Radhanagar Beach, scuba diving at Elephant Beach and sea-walking are already paid for. The difficulty rating is Easy — no trekking, no altitude, no summit pushes. The rhythm is deliberately unhurried: two active water days, one history day, one slow-water day, one open day and a gentle departure. Expect 24–31°C throughout, salt in your hair by mid-morning, and dinner finished before nine.

## Why Visit

The Andamans sit closer to Myanmar than to the Indian mainland, and it shows. The water off Havelock runs jade to deep blue, the sand at Radhanagar is powder-fine, and the forest behind it is genuine rainforest — padauk and gurjan, not planted palms. This is one of the few places in India where a complete beginner can be breathing underwater on a live coral reef within an hour of stepping onto a boat, and where a sea-walk on the seabed is a half-day activity rather than an expedition.

The second layer is human and much heavier. Port Blair holds the Cellular Jail, the colonial prison where Indian political prisoners were held in solitary confinement, and Ross Island (Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose Dweep), the former British headquarters now half-swallowed by banyan roots and patrolled by deer. Doing both gives the holiday an unusual shape: mornings of almost absurd prettiness, evenings that ask something of you. Add settler cuisine from Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Punjab layered over island seafood, and you have a destination that rewards six days rather than a long weekend.

## Getting There & Around

Everyone arrives by air. Veer Savarkar International Airport at Port Blair is the single gateway, with direct flights from Chennai, Kolkata, Delhi, Bengaluru and Hyderabad depending on season; Chennai and Kolkata are the shortest hops at roughly two to two and a half hours. Flights are **not** included — TravoAI can price them separately by distance on request. Book early for the October–March peak, and prefer morning arrivals so you can connect onward the same day.

Port Blair to Havelock is a sea crossing of about 55 km. Private air-conditioned catamaran ferries typically take 90 minutes to two hours; government ferries are slower and cheaper. Sailings cluster in the morning and early afternoon and sell out weeks ahead in season, so treat the ferry booking as urgent, not incidental. Because the package's transport line covers private sedan transfers and sightseeing — a road service — confirm in writing with your booking agent whether inter-island ferry tickets sit inside the ₹70,000 or are billed separately.

On land you are looked after: airport pickup, jetty transfers and all sightseeing runs are by private sedan with a driver, a genuine luxury on Havelock's single main road when the afternoon sun is at its worst. Scooters are available for hire if you want independence; ride slowly, watch for sand on bends, and carry your licence.

## Day-by-Day Deep Dive

**Day 1 — Arrival and an easy start.** The morning is logistics done comfortably: landing at Veer Savarkar airport, a private sedan waiting, and a short transfer to the jetty for the crossing to Havelock. Indian nationals need no permit for Port Blair, Havelock or Neil; foreign nationals are normally issued a Restricted Area Permit, so check current rules before you travel. By early afternoon you are checking into Radhanagar Bayview Resort and eating a late lunch. The late afternoon is the day's whole point: Radhanagar Beach, Beach No. 7, a two-kilometre arc of white sand backed by rainforest, with your guide along for orientation. Swim the shallow shelf, then stay for a sunset that lands squarely over the water. Dinner is relaxed and early.

**Day 2 — Scuba at Elephant Beach and sea-walking.** The headline day starts early, because the sea is flattest before mid-morning. A speedboat runs from Havelock jetty to Elephant Beach in 20–30 minutes; the jungle trail alternative is muddy and often closed after rain. Your discover-scuba session needs no certification — a beach briefing, mask and regulator practice in waist-deep water, then a guided descent to roughly 8–12 metres with an instructor holding you steady. Expect staghorn and brain corals, parrotfish, clownfish in anemones and possibly a passing turtle. After a break, the sea-walk takes over: a weighted helmet feeds surface air while you walk the seabed, which suits non-swimmers. Both passes are covered. The evening is deliberately empty — shower, rest, let your ears settle.

**Day 3 — Cellular Jail and Ross Island.** Ferry back towards Port Blair in the morning and let the day change register. Mid-morning, take the boat to Ross Island, twenty minutes offshore, where the British administrative capital has been reclaimed by banyan and ficus roots growing through the church, bakery and ballroom, and spotted deer wander the paths. Many operators pair this sailing with North Bay, the coral-viewing point known for glass-bottom boats and snorkelling — ask your guide whether yours includes it. In the afternoon, walk the Cellular Jail: the surviving wings, the central tower, the gallows and the solitary cells. Stay for the evening light-and-sound show in the courtyard. It is a quiet dinner afterwards, and it should be.

**Day 4 — Kayaking through the mangroves.** A soft-adventure day with a different texture. Morning sessions launch into the mangrove creeks — glassy water at first light, flat paddling, no experience needed beyond a willingness to get wet. You glide through tunnels of stilt-rooted rhizophora, spotting mudskippers, kingfishers, mangrove crabs and, if the tide cooperates, a monitor lizard on a root. Guides often run a bioluminescence variant on moonless nights, when disturbed plankton glow around the paddle; ask whether your dates suit it. The afternoon is free, and most travellers take the sedan to Kalapathar Beach on Havelock's eastern edge, where black rocks meet turquoise shallows and crowds thin. Evening is a good slot for the package's signature dinner.

**Day 5 — Leisure day, or a second island.** This day is open on purpose, and how you spend it defines your trip. The popular choice is Neil Island (Shaheed Dweep), about an hour by ferry: Bharatpur Beach for snorkelling, Laxmanpur for sunset, and the Natural Rock Bridge, reachable only around low tide, so check the tide chart. The more demanding option, from Port Blair, is Baratang limestone caves — an early convoy along the Andaman Trunk Road through the Jarawa Tribal Reserve, a boat through mangrove creeks, then a short walk. Photographing or interacting with Jarawa people is a serious offence; do neither. Chidiya Tapu, 25 km south of Port Blair, is the gentler sunset alternative. Or simply stay put and swim.

**Day 6 — Souvenirs and departure.** Breakfast at leisure, then a final morning shaped around your flight time. The plan is Aberdeen Bazaar, Port Blair's main market grid, for shell and pearl craft, coconut-shell curios, wooden boats, spices and local honey. Sagarika Emporium, the government-run outlet, is the safer buy for fixed prices and provenance; independent pearl stalls are cheaper but demand judgement. Do not buy raw coral or protected shell and turtle products — they are illegal to carry out and will be seized. Your sedan then runs you to the airport, fifteen to twenty minutes from the bazaar. One firm rule: leave at least 18–24 hours between your last dive and your flight, which is exactly why the diving sits on Day 2.

## Where to Stay

Your five nights are at Radhanagar Bayview Resort, a 4-star resort and boutique property rated 4.6, positioned for easy access to Havelock's western beach belt. Expect what this tier delivers across the islands: low-rise cottage or block-style rooms with air-conditioning, tea-coffee facilities, a balcony or sit-out, a pool, an in-house multi-cuisine restaurant, and a travel desk that will handle ferry re-timings and dive bookings. Rooms tend to be generous, and sea-facing categories carry a premium worth asking about at booking rather than on arrival.

The trade-off is location versus convenience. Havelock's resorts spread along one road, so staying near Radhanagar buys sunset walks but puts you 10–12 km from the jetty and village restaurants. With private transfers included, that matters far less than it otherwise would. Power cuts and uneven water pressure happen at island properties even at four stars, and most run generators. Travelling for an occasion? Mention it when booking — decorations and a private beach-side dinner are usually arranged for a modest supplement.

## Food & Dining

Seafood is the reason to eat out. Grilled lobster is the island indulgence, usually priced by weight and best confirmed before it hits the grill. Fish curry with coconut — snapper, grouper or tuna in a thin, sour, coconut-milk gravy — is the everyday classic, and prawn masala appears on almost every menu. The settler layer is the surprise: Bengali fish preparations, Tamil rice-and-sambar meals and even Amritsari kulcha, brought by Punjabi settlers, sit comfortably beside the local catch. Tender coconut is sold everywhere and is the best rehydration you will find after a dive.

Your package covers daily breakfast plus one signature dinner, typically a set or curated menu at the resort. Every other lunch and dinner is on you. Havelock's Beach No. 5 area and Govind Nagar hold the widest cluster of independent cafés and shacks; Port Blair's Aberdeen area is stronger for South Indian thalis and Bengali fish. Vegetarians eat well — dosa, thali and paneer are universal — while strict Jain and vegan travellers should call ahead, since coconut-oil kitchens often share equipment with seafood. Alcohol is legally sold, though choice is limited outside licensed resorts.

## Culture & Etiquette

Andaman society is almost entirely a settler society — Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Malayali and Punjabi communities alongside Nicobarese and other indigenous groups — and the shared street language is Hindi, with English widely understood in tourism. A simple *namaste* travels fine.

Beachwear belongs on the beach. Cover up before walking into a market, a village lane or a restaurant in town, and dress modestly at temples, churches and gurdwaras, removing footwear where indicated. At the Cellular Jail, remember you are inside a memorial: keep your voice down and skip posed photographs in the cells. Photography is broadly fine at beaches and monuments, but monument still and video camera charges are excluded from your package, so carry small change. Never photograph indigenous people, tribal reserve areas or defence installations — the islands host significant military infrastructure and restrictions are enforced.

Tipping is customary but not aggressive. Around ₹300–₹500 a day for a driver, ₹500–₹800 for a full-day guide, and 5–10% at restaurants without a service charge is a fair benchmark.

## Budget Breakdown (₹)

The ₹70,000 is a package price for two travellers — roughly ₹35,000 per head for six days — and reads best as a bundle rather than a line-item invoice. It covers five nights at Radhanagar Bayview Resort in the 4-star tier; daily breakfast plus one signature dinner; all private sedan transfers, including airport and jetty pickups, and sightseeing runs; a certified local guide on the main sightseeing days; and entry and experience passes for Radhanagar Beach, the discover-scuba session at Elephant Beach and the sea-walk. Those two water activities alone typically run into several thousand rupees per person when bought independently, which is where much of the value sits.

Excluded: flights, travel insurance, personal expenses, tips, optional activities and monument camera charges. Budget realistically for the rest. Return airfares from mainland metros commonly land between ₹9,000 and ₹22,000 per person depending on how early you book and how close you fly to the December–January peak. Lunches and non-included dinners typically run ₹1,200–₹2,500 a day for two, more if lobster appears. Add ferry tickets if they are not bundled, monument and light-and-sound entry of a few hundred rupees each, kayaking, any Neil Island or Baratang trip, and shopping. A comfortable allowance for two, excluding flights, is ₹20,000–₹30,000 across the six days. To save, skip the second island and eat in the village; to upgrade, ask about a sea-facing category and a private beach dinner.

## Best Time & Weather

The island season runs October to April, and every one of those months is recommended for this package. Conditions hold at roughly 24–31°C with high humidity year-round; what changes is the sea. October and early November are green and freshly washed after the monsoon, with fewer crowds and softer rates, though showers and choppier crossings persist. December and January are the peak — driest air, calmest water, best underwater visibility, and prices and ferry demand to match, especially over Christmas and New Year. February and March are the divers' sweet spot: warm water, excellent visibility, thinner crowds. April is still very good but noticeably hotter by afternoon.

May to September is the southwest monsoon: heavy rain, rough seas, frequent ferry cancellations and many dive operators closed. Avoid it for a trip of this shape. Sunrise comes remarkably early here, around 5 a.m., and darkness falls by about 5.30 p.m., because the islands run on Indian Standard Time far east of its meridian. Plan sightseeing early and accept early nights.

## Packing List

Pack light, quick-drying and sun-aware. Two or three swimsuits so one is always dry, cotton and linen clothes, a rash guard for reef time, a light cover-up for towns, and one smart-casual outfit for your signature dinner. Footwear: flip-flops for the beach, reef shoes or old sneakers for rocky entries, and a closed pair for mangrove and jungle stretches.

Bring reef-safe mineral sunscreen at SPF 50 or higher, a wide-brimmed hat, polarised sunglasses, strong insect repellent for dusk and mangrove trips, and a dry bag for boats. Carry printed and digital copies of ID, tickets and vouchers, plus medication with prescriptions. Four things travellers here routinely forget: a power bank, since island power cuts are common; enough cash, because ATMs on Havelock are few and often out of service; motion-sickness tablets for the ferry; and a waterproof phone pouch.

## Safety & Health

The dominant risks are sun, sea and complacency. Heat and humidity dehydrate you faster than you notice, so drink steadily and stick to bottled or properly filtered water. Sunburn on a boat is brutal even under cloud, so reapply after every swim. Swim between flags where lifeguards are posted, respect red flags, and remember that Radhanagar's shelf drops away and currents shift; leave the water if you feel yourself being pulled sideways.

For diving, declare any asthma, heart condition, recent surgery or pregnancy honestly on the medical form, dive only with an instructor you have watched check the gear, and keep the 18–24 hour no-fly window after your last dive. Ask your dive operator where the nearest recompression facility is before you get in the water. Port Blair holds the islands' main hospitals and referral care; Havelock has smaller primary facilities, so anything serious means a transfer. The national emergency number is 112. Roads are narrow and unlit after dark; if you hire a scooter, wear the helmet. Travel insurance is excluded here — buy a policy that explicitly covers recreational scuba to your planned depth.

## Responsible Travel

Coral is a living animal and Andaman reefs are already under heat stress. Never stand on, touch or kick coral, keep fins clear of the reef, and choose mineral over chemical sunscreen. Do not feed fish, chase turtles, or ask a boatman to push closer to wildlife than it wants you to be. Take nothing from the beach — collecting coral, shells or sand is damaging and, for protected species, illegal.

Plastic is the islands' hardest problem, because almost nothing can be processed locally. Carry a refillable bottle, refuse single-use straws and cutlery, and pack out whatever you bring to a beach. Spend where the money stays: buy from Aberdeen Bazaar traders and Sagarika Emporium, hire local guides and boat crews, and eat in village restaurants rather than only at the resort. Above all, respect the tribal reserves absolutely — no photographs, no gifts, no interaction.

## FAQ

**Are flights to Port Blair included?**
No. Airfare to the gateway is separate, along with travel insurance, personal expenses, tips, optional activities and monument camera charges. TravoAI can price flights by distance on request.

**Do I need a permit for the Andamans?**
Indian citizens do not need one for Port Blair, Havelock or Neil, though photo ID is required at jetties. Foreign nationals are normally issued a Restricted Area Permit, and Baratang needs a separate checkpost permit. Rules change, so verify current requirements before booking.

**Can a complete beginner scuba dive?**
Yes. The Elephant Beach session is a discover-scuba dive requiring no certification — you are briefed, given confined-water practice, then guided by an instructor throughout. If a mask makes you uneasy, the sea-walk covered in the same package is the gentler alternative.

**Is this suitable for children or non-swimmers?**
Largely yes. The difficulty rating is Easy, and beaches, Ross Island, the Cellular Jail and kayaking all work for families. Dive operators usually set a minimum age of around ten for try-dives, and sea-walks have their own limits, so confirm ages in advance.

**How good is mobile network and internet?**
Better than its reputation since the submarine fibre link, but still uneven. Port Blair is generally reliable; Havelock can be patchy, and remote beaches often have nothing. Assume you will be partly offline and tell people at home.

**What is the cancellation policy?**
Full refund up to 15 days before departure, 50% between 7 and 14 days prior, and no refund within 6 days of travel. Date changes depend on availability and any fare difference.

**Can the package be customised?**
Yes. Hotels, duration and add-on experiences can all be tailored, with the price adjusting accordingly. Common changes are adding a Neil Island night, upgrading the room category, or extending to seven days.

**Is it good for solo travellers?**
It is priced and configured for two, so a solo booking carries a single-occupancy supplement. The experience itself is very solo-friendly, with dive centres and group boat trips making company easy to find.

## Final Word

Six days is enough to do the Andamans properly without rushing, and this itinerary spends them well: one beach that deserves its reputation, one morning underwater that most travellers call the best hour of the trip, one afternoon with real historical weight, and enough unclaimed time to follow your own instincts on Day 5. Private transfers and pre-paid water activities remove precisely the friction that spoils island holidays. Book flights and ferries early, keep the last dive well clear of the flight home, and let the islands set the pace.
